title: AAC Export Became M4A? Check the Codec and Container
description: Understand why AAC audio can be saved as M4A, check the actual codec, and choose a compatible sharing copy on iPhone without renaming the file.
direct: An AAC export can correctly end in .m4a. AAC describes the encoded audio. M4A describes the file container, which can also hold Apple Lossless audio.
figureAlt: A card marked AAC sits inside an M4A sleeve, illustrating audio encoding inside a file container.

cards.decision.heading: Read the file information
cards.decision.body: If you asked for AAC and received M4A, first check the audio information in a trusted player or editor. Do not rename the file merely to make the letters match: a filename change does not convert the contents.
sections.detail-0-0.heading: One extension, more than one codec
sections.detail-0-0.body: The UK National Archives identifies AAC-based M4A and notes that the extension is also used by Apple Lossless files. An M4A name therefore does not establish whether the audio is lossy. Likewise, selecting another container does not restore detail that an earlier lossy encode discarded.
sections.detail-1-0.heading: Choose compatibility before converting
sections.detail-1-0.body: Its current listing includes audio conversion and MP3, M4A, WAV and AAC handling. Export tools require Pro.
sections.detail-1-1.heading: Check the exact format request
sections.detail-1-1.body: This guide does not promise raw AAC/ADTS export or a lossless rewrap option. If the existing file plays correctly and the recipient accepts it, another conversion may be unnecessary. When MP3 is explicitly required, use a real MP3 conversion and check that new file rather than renaming the M4A.
faqs.reader-question-1.heading: Does .m4a always mean the audio is lossy?
faqs.reader-question-1.body: No. An M4A can contain AAC or Apple Lossless audio. Check the codec in a trusted player or inspector.
faqs.reader-question-2.heading: A form asks for .aac. Can I just change the filename?
faqs.reader-question-2.body: No. Ask whether the form accepts AAC audio in an M4A container or requires a raw AAC stream. Use a workflow that produces the required file.

steps.step-1.text: Check what the recipient actually requires: AAC audio in M4A, an MP3 file, or a specific raw AAC stream. These are different requirements.
steps.step-2.text: For an ordinary sharing copy, use the available conversion format in Audio Compressor MP3 Converter. Keep the source and export a separate file.
steps.step-3.text: Open the saved copy in the receiving app. Confirm playback, duration and the reported encoding. If a specialist system demands raw AAC, do not assume that an M4A export meets that requirement.
